abstract: Climate change threatens coral reefs globally, highlighting the need to understand mechanisms underlying coral holobiont resilience. Intertidal corals exhibit superior heat tolerance, yet the role of associated microbiomes remains unclear. By integrating field surveys, heat-stress experiments, and metagenomics, we compared intertidal and subtidal Porites lutea microbiomes. Our results show that intertidal P. lutea host bacterial communities are enriched in generalists with broad niche breadths and exhibit high functional redundancy in stress-response pathways. Under acute thermal stress, intertidal corals showed greater thermotolerance than subtidal corals. Concurrently, intertidal coral-associated bacterial communities maintained relatively stable taxonomic composition and functional integrity. Across habitats, preservation of photosynthetic efficiency (Fv/Fm) in the coral holobiont under heat stress was associated with higher bacterial generalist richness and functional redundancy. Together, these results suggest that long-term environmental variability may be associated with microbiome features consistent with functional buffering and holobiont stability. These findings may inform the design of synthetic microbial consortia to improve coral resilience under warming oceans.
